content: Rabies is transmitted exclusively when the virus is introduced into bite wounds, open skin cuts, or mucous membranes through saliva or other potentially infectious materials, such as neural tissue. Any questions regarding potential exposures should be promptly directed to state or local public health authorities. Public health education is a critical component of rabies prevention and control. This includes ongoing public awareness campaigns, responsible pet ownership, routine veterinary care, and professional continuing education. Most animal and human exposures to rabies can be prevented by educating the public about transmission routes, avoiding contact with wildlife, and ensuring proper veterinary care. Prompt recognition and reporting of potential exposures to medical professionals and public health authorities are essential. Human rabies can be prevented by either avoiding exposure to rabid animals or by providing exposed individuals with immediate local wound treatment combined with the administration of human rabies immune globulin and vaccine. The rationale for pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, as well as their administration details, are outlined in the current recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). These recommendations, along with information on the local and regional epidemiology of animal rabies and the availability of human rabies biologics, can be obtained from state health departments. Local governments should implement and maintain effective programs to ensure the vaccination of all dogs, cats, and ferrets, as well as the removal of stray and unwanted animals. In the United States, such measures have significantly reduced laboratory-confirmed rabies cases in dogs from 6,949 in 1947 to 76 in 2005. Since more rabies cases are reported annually in cats (269 in 2005) than in dogs, cat vaccination should be mandatory. Animal shelters and animal-control authorities should establish policies to ensure that adopted animals are vaccinated against rabies. Vaccination procedures and licensed animal vaccines are detailed in Parts II and III of this compendium. Rabies vaccinations may also be administered under veterinary supervision to animals in shelters before release. Veterinarians signing rabies certificates must ensure that the person administering the vaccine is identified on the certificate and is appropriately trained in vaccine storage, handling, administration, and adverse event management. This ensures accountability for proper vaccination. Within 28 days of initial vaccination, peak rabies virus antibody titers are achieved, and the animal is considered immunized. An animal is considered currently vaccinated and immunized if the initial vaccination was administered at least 28 days prior or if booster vaccinations have been given according to the compendium's guidelines. Regardless of the animal's age at initial vaccination, a booster should be administered one year later. There is no laboratory or epidemiologic data to support annual or biennial administration of 3or 4-year vaccines following the initial series. A rapid anamnestic response is expected, and an animal is considered currently vaccinated immediately after a booster vaccination. All dogs, cats, and ferrets should be vaccinated and revaccinated against rabies according to Part III of this compendium. If a previously vaccinated animal is overdue for a booster, it should be revaccinated. Immediately following the booster, the animal is considered currently vaccinated and should be placed on a vaccination schedule according to the labeled duration of the vaccine used. Livestock, particularly those of high value or those in public settings such as petting zoos or fairs, should be considered for vaccination. Horses traveling interstate should also be currently vaccinated against rabies. Wild animals or hybrids (offspring of wild animals crossbred with domestic animals) should not be kept as pets, as recommended by the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA). Handling and consumption of tissues from exposed animals may pose a risk for rabies transmission. The risk depends on factors such as the site of exposure, the amount of virus present, the severity of wounds, and whether contaminated tissue is excised. If an exposed animal is to be slaughtered for consumption, it should be done immediately after exposure. Barrier precautions should be used by individuals handling the animal, and all tissues should be thoroughly cooked. Federal guidelines for meat inspectors require that any animal known to have been exposed to rabies within eight months be rejected for slaughter. USDA Food and Inspection Service (FSIS) meat inspectors should be notified if such exposures occur in food animals before slaughter. In infected animals, the rabies virus may be widely distributed in tissues. Tissues and products from a rabid animal should not be used for human or animal consumption. However, pasteurization temperatures inactivate the rabies virus, so consuming pasteurized milk or thoroughly cooked animal products does not constitute rabies exposure. Multiple rabid animals in a herd or herbivore-to-herbivore transmission is uncommon; therefore, restricting the rest of the herd if a single animal has been exposed to or infected by rabies is usually unnecessary. Other mammals exposed to a rabid animal should be euthanized immediately. Animals maintained in USDA-licensed research facilities or accredited zoological parks should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Rabies virus may be excreted in the saliva of infected dogs, cats, and ferrets during illness and/or for only a few days before illness or death. A healthy dog, cat, or ferret that bites a person should be confined and observed daily for 10 days. Rabies vaccination should not be administered during the observation period to avoid confusing rabies signs with potential vaccine side effects. Animals in confinement should be evaluated by a veterinarian at the first sign of illness. Any illness in the animal should be reported immediately to the local health department. Stray or unwanted dogs, cats, or ferrets that bite a person may be euthanized immediately, and the head submitted for rabies examination. Other biting animals that may have exposed a person to rabies should be reported immediately to the local health department. Management of animals other than dogs, cats, and ferrets depends on the species, the circumstances of the bite, the epidemiology of rabies in the area, the biting animal's history, current health status, and potential exposure to rabies. Previous vaccination of these animals may not preclude the need for euthanasia and testing. The emergence of new rabies virus variants and the introduction of nonindigenous viruses pose significant risks to humans, domestic animals, and wildlife. In such situations, the public health response should be rapid and comprehensive, including measures such as characterizing the virus at a reference laboratory, identifying and controlling the source of introduction, enhancing laboratory-based surveillance in wild and domestic animals, increasing animal rabies vaccination rates, restricting the movement of animals at risk, evaluating the need for vector population reduction, coordinating a multi-agency response, and providing public and professional outreach and education. Vaccines used in state and local rabies control programs should have at least a 3-year duration of immunity. This is the most effective method of increasing the proportion of immunized dogs and cats in any population. There is no laboratory or epidemiologic data to support annual or biennial administration of 3or 4-year vaccines following the initial series.
